newsitem.title: CANADA: Plugged In: Shimmering mirage of a speedy Internet.
newsitem.headline: Plugged In: Shimmering mirage of a speedy Internet.

text.p: Like a mirage shimmering in the desert, cable and telephone companies have been holding out the promise of speedy Internet access.
There is probably not a dedicated surfer who does not utter a prayer to that mirage every time a fascinating but graphic-heavy Web site oozes painfully onto the screen.
But for many long-suffering surfers, the promise of decent download speeds always seems to be coming sometime next year.

The big companies, be they cable or telco, follow the same pattern: first, the launching of a trial for a new Internet service for a few lucky people and then vague predictions abut when everyone else will get to subscribe.
Canada's cable television companies again whetted the appetite of Internet types on November 12 with the announcement of a national rollout of a high speed cable Internet service.

The cable companies this time, however, said they were past the testing stage and would deliver the service, called Wave (www.wave.ca), over the next few months on a neighborhood-by-neighborhood basis across Canada. Full installation of Wave would still take a couple of years. Since Canada is one of the most cabled countries on earth, it was a significant announcement that two million Canadians were on the verge of having access to rapid Internet access -- which could put them a step ahead of many others in the international Internet community.

In a slick presentation in Toronto, the cable group wowed the crowd by rapidly downloading an image of a painting over the cable service, while the same picture over a regular phone line arrived in the usual tardy manner.
"Tomorrow it's going to be amazing," read the equally slick Wave brochure.

Initially there were predictions that getting the Internet over your cable television line with its special modem would deliver the Internet some 1,000 times faster that the normal 28.8 bits per second modem.

Cable officials, however, said that after a trial in Newmarket, Ontario, near Toronto, they saw the Internet coming in about 10 times faster. They said that would be much faster than the special digital ISDN telephone line now available and a little slower than the latest toy offered by the telephone companies, the digital ADSL line. They also promised a faster cable system would come in time to surpass ADSL.

The service does not come cheap. At C$55 (US$41) a month (and a not inconsequential installation fee of C$150 (US$113)), the fee is two to three times that charged by a regular Internet service provider.
But Wave can be left on 24 hours a day, comes with up to five e-mail addresses, a choice of browsers and room to launch your own Web page.

That all sounds wonderful but there is considerable skepticism whether cable companies in Canada -- or in the United States -- will be able to deliver on the promises any time soon. Critics wonder how the cable companies can finance it all when it was unclear whether there was demand for such a premium service.

Telephone companies, such as the U.S. Baby Bells, have been talking up ADSL and launching a slew of trials. That could prove tough competition for cable companies, especially in Canada, where some cable firms are struggling to raise the hundreds of millions of dollars needed to fund the expansion of their systems to make it Internet-ready.

But Frank Cotter, a vice president at Canada's largest cable system, Rogers Communications Inc, believes demand will snowball. He said that in the Newmarket trial some five percent of cable customers signed up for Wave.
"It took cellular phones seven years to get to five percent and cellular is considered a huge success," he said.
